items.passage: We arrived at the Posillipo pool at seven, because Elisa said the salt water was flattest before the swim club came. My brother brought goggles. She confiscated them. Fishermen's sons had learned it on this coast before anyone sold inflatable rings, she said, and now the sons sold inflatable rings. My brother sank eleven times. On the twelfth try he drifted for perhaps nine seconds, arms out, staring at the sky. Elisa did not clap. We talked about the bride's lace, the rain, the price of a ticket to Dublin. We did not talk about the choir loft at St. Nicholas, where I had stood every Sunday until my brother's funeral. When the fiddlers paused, he leaned over, opened the hymnal to a page whose corner someone had long ago folded down, and went back to his cake. I closed it. Later, as the guests rose for the toast, I opened it again to the folded page and laid it face up on my chair.

A) the narrator's tentative move back toward a subject the two leave unspoken.
B) a handy object the narrator uses to cool herself in the crowded hall.
C) the narrator's polite ease with social chatter at the wedding breakfast.
D) a quarrel between the narrator and the priest that she finally settles.
### lit40-hard-03-001 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language · 요청 난이도 hard · hard 기준: 관용 해석으로 풀 수 없고, 오답이 비유의 다른 속성에서 나온 그럴듯한 해석이며 정답은 두 곳 이상의 단서가 정한다

Folded twice and then once more, Salma's invitation lay on the planks of the dock where she had set it, weighted with a lemon. Her new daughter-in-law had come to Marrakesh only that spring, and the lake below the rented villa was the one corner of the household where nobody followed anyone. Each evening the bride walked to the end of the dock, unfolded the card, read the date of Salma's luncheon, and folded it again along the same creases. She did not answer it, and she did not throw it into the water. Wolfram, watching from the terrace, called the card his mother's paper anchor. Salma heard him and went on shelling beans. On the third evening the bride carried the lemon back to the kitchen, sliced it, and served it with the tea, leaving the card on the boards with nothing on top of it.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “paper anchor” most nearly suggests that the invitation is
A) a demand that feels much too heavy for the bride to bear
B) a pull that keeps drawing the bride back to an unsettled choice
C) a boundary that marks how far out the bride may walk
D) a weight that holds the card down against the lake wind
### lit40-hard-03-002 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language · 요청 난이도 hard · hard 기준: 관용 해석으로 풀 수 없고, 오답이 비유의 다른 속성에서 나온 그럴듯한 해석이며 정답은 두 곳 이상의 단서가 정한다
[지문]
When the ice truck stopped coming to the harbor in Colombo, Ayita began packing the morning catch in sawdust from the boatyard. Her family's stall had sold fish on the same corner for forty years, and the shutter now stuck halfway each dawn while the newer stalls rolled theirs up with a motor. Faisal, who had fished beside her grandfather, came by every morning, lifted the shutter the last few inches with his shoulder, and left without buying anything. Buyers still came, mostly old ones, and the scale still swung. One wet morning Faisal called the stall a lantern with the wick cut short. Ayita wrote the phrase on the back of a receipt. The following week she ordered a new shutter spring, then put the receipt in the cash tin beneath the coins, where she would see it each time she made change.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “a lantern with the wick cut short” most nearly suggests that the stall is
A) a source of comfort that still warms the harbor families
B) a light too dim to draw new buyers to the corner
C) a business still working but nearing the end of its run
D) a business whose worn fixtures need steady repair to function
